title: Research Bite #60: Teacher-Student Relationships and Student Outcomes
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #60 covers Valentin Emslander, Doris Holzberger, Sverre Berg Ofstad, Antoine Fischbach, and Ronny Scherer's 'Teacher-Student Relationships and Student Outcomes: A Systematic Second-Order Meta-Analytic Review,' published in Psychological Bulletin (2025, Vol. 151, No. 3, pp. 365-397). This is a meta-analysis of meta-analyses: the team synthesized 26 existing meta-analyses (119 meta-analytic effect sizes) spanning over 70 years of research and roughly 2.64 million pre-K through K-12 students, to evaluate how teacher-student relationships (TSRs) relate to eight clusters of student outcomes -- academic achievement, academic emotions, appropriate behavior, behavior problems, executive function and self-control, motivation, school belonging/engagement, and well-being. Positive TSRs showed consistently large, significant relationships across nearly all of these clusters, while negative relationships (marked by conflict or dependency) correlated with increased behavior problems. The effect was strongest for middle and high school students, suggesting the relational bond matters more, not less, as students get older -- a finding that cuts against the intuition that relationship-building matters most in early years.
points: As a second-order meta-analysis of 26 meta-analyses (2.64 million students), this is about as strong an evidence base as exists in education research -- TSR quality is not a soft, marginal variable but one with large effects across eight distinct outcome domains.

The finding that TSR importance grows through middle and high school, not just in early grades, challenges the common practice of front-loading relationship-building efforts into the primary years and easing off afterward.

Negative relationships (conflict, dependency) tracking specifically with behavior problems -- rather than just lower achievement -- suggests behavior interventions should examine relational quality before defaulting to consequence-based systems.

The breadth of outcomes affected (achievement, emotions, behavior, executive function, motivation, belonging, well-being) means TSR quality functions less like one lever among many and more like a foundational condition that other interventions depend on.

The study's own recommendation -- specialised teacher training focused on relationship-building -- treats TSR quality as a trainable skill, not a fixed personality trait, which is itself a high-impact reframe for school professional development.
quotes: This second-order meta-analysis synthesises over 70 years of educational research to evaluate how teacher-student relationships (TSRs) impact various student outcomes.

By analysing 26 existing meta-analyses covering approximately 2.64 million students, the authors confirm that positive interactions significantly boost academic achievement, motivation, and well-being.
Conversely, the research highlights how negative relationships, characterised by conflict or dependency, correlate with increased behavioural problems.
The findings indicate that these social bonds are particularly influential for middle and high school students, suggesting that the importance of the TSR grows as children age.
Ultimately, the study serves as a comprehensive guide for policymakers and educators, advocating for specialised teacher training to foster classroom environments built on safety and belonging.
